The testing was conducted at the NASA Glenn Research Center W-7 High Speed Multi-Stage Axial Compressor Facility.
The compressor had a rotor size of 20 to 22 inches and was driven by a 15,000 hp motor.
The 1-stage configuration included a strut, IGV, Rotor 1, Stator 1, and a de-swirl vane.
The 2-stage configuration added a Rotor 2 and Stator 2 to the 1-stage configuration.
The IGV, Stator 1, and Stator 2 were variable stagger vanes.

Detailed instrumentation included inlet and exit rakes, vane leading edge pressure and temperature probes, casing and hub static pressure taps, and traverses with 5-hole probes, Kulite pressure transducers, and hot wire anemometry.
The 2-stage configuration choked at a lower mass flow rate than the 1-stage configuration.
Rotor 1 performance was negligibly affected by the presence of the second stage.
The Stage 1 efficiency was found to be low relative to the design intent.
The likely cause of the Stage 1 performance deficit was a stage mismatch issue due to Stage 2 choking.
Previous test experience had indicated a performance deficit in this compressor at high speed, which was not captured by RANS/URANS CFD.

Potential explanations for the previously measured performance deficit included unanticipated losses through the gooseneck, Rotor 1 wake, Rotor 2 inlet/strut/IGV mixing, and Rotor 2 bow shock interaction with Stage 1.
The goal of the NASA Environmentally Responsible Aviation Project (ERA) was to identify and mature technologies that can simultaneously meet metrics for noise, emissions, and fuel burn.
ERA system studies have shown potential for up to 2.5% reduction in Thrust Specific Fuel Consumption by increasing core compressor pressure ratio by 30%.
Increased loading of the core compressor can introduce aerodynamic losses and decreased efficiency in the front stages.
